text: You already know the headline rule from Course 3: every applicable ACL must pass, an AND across ACLs, never an OR. This lesson goes one level deeper, into what happens when ACLs exist at more than one level of a table's inheritance hierarchy.

Task is a base table. Incident, Problem, and Change Request all extend it, and they inherit task's ACLs along with its fields. Define one ACL on task for the read operation, requiring the itil role, and that single rule governs read access on all three extended tables at once -- without you ever touching their own ACL lists.

But inheritance is a default, not an absolute. If an ACL also exists directly on incident for the same read operation, ServiceNow uses that incident-level ACL for Incident records instead of the task-level one -- it does not run both and AND them together. Here, the incident-level script keeps the itil role requirement but also lets the caller see their own ticket. Problem and Change still fall back to the task-level rule, since neither has its own override.

The real precedence rule is: most specific ACL wins. ServiceNow checks the exact table first, then walks up the inheritance chain -- parent, grandparent, up to task -- and stops at the first level where a matching ACL exists for that operation. A base-table ACL is the default for everything beneath it, right up until a more specific one takes over for one particular table.

This is a genuinely common source of confusion. An admin edits the task-level read ACL, tests it against an Incident, and sees no change -- because Incident was never using that ACL to begin with; it has its own, more specific one. Before concluding an ACL isn't working, query sys_security_acl for both table equals task and table equals incident, filtered to the same operation, and confirm which one is actually in effect.
Most specific wins, and it's an override, not an AND. Next up: scripted ACL conditions, and why a slow ACL script becomes a performance problem for the entire instance, not just one feature.
